summary.text: The Battle of the Somme was a First World War battle fought from 1 July to 18 November 1916 in France by British and French armies against the German Empire.
More than three million men fought, and more than one million were wounded or killed, making it one of the deadliest battles in human history.
The Allies pushed 6.2 miles (10 km) into German-occupied territory along most of the front, but did not achieve their operational objectives.

items.explain: The plan was reduced to a limited offensive to relieve pressure at Verdun and inflict attrition on the German armies.

paragraphs.heading: A battle by a French river
paragraphs.text: The Battle of the Somme, also called the Somme offensive, was a First World War battle. Armies of the British Empire and the French Republic fought the German Empire there from 1 July to 18 November 1916, on both banks of the upper river Somme in France. Over three million men took part, and more than a million of them were killed or wounded. That toll puts it among the deadliest battles people have ever fought.

paragraphs.heading: The plan
paragraphs.text: The Allies settled their strategy for 1916 at the Chantilly Conference in December 1915. Russian, Italian, French and British armies would all attack at the same time, so that the Central Powers had no quiet spells in which to shift troops from one front to another. The Somme attack was the joint French and British share of that plan. At first the French were to do most of the fighting, with the British Fourth Army helping on the northern side.

paragraphs.heading: Verdun changes everything
paragraphs.text: On 21 February 1916 the German army opened the Battle of Verdun against the French. Defending Verdun cost the French so much that they moved divisions meant for the Somme, leaving 13 French divisions beside 20 British ones. The British attack, planned as the supporting effort, became the main one. By 31 May the hope of a decisive win had shrunk to a limited attack to ease the pressure on Verdun and wear down the German armies.

paragraphs.heading: The first day
paragraphs.text: On 1 July the German 2nd Army was badly beaten by the French Sixth Army and by the British Fourth Army along part of the line. Yet the British lost 57,470 men that day, 19,240 of them killed, the worst losses the British Army has ever suffered. Most fell to the north, between the Albert–Bapaume road and Gommecourt, where the Germans had put their main defensive effort. Many of the British soldiers were wartime volunteers mixed with what was left of the pre-war army.

paragraphs.heading: New machines, mixed results
paragraphs.text: Air power mattered a great deal at the Somme, and the tank was used in battle for the first time there, in September. Both were new technology, though, and they proved unreliable. The battle showed how deadly mechanized warfare could be, a kind of fighting that had begun in the mid-1800s.

paragraphs.heading: What it achieved
paragraphs.text: By the end, British and French troops had pushed 10 km (6.2 miles) into German-held land along most of the front, the most ground they had won since the 1914 First Battle of the Marne. Still, they did not take Péronne or Bapaume, so the operational goals were missed and the Germans held on there through the winter. In March 1917 the Germans pulled back about 40 km to the Hindenburg Line. People still argue over whether the battle was necessary and what it really did.
